column4: The ayah names night itself لِبَاسًا, exactly confirming the section's image of entering the night as one enters a garment.
Allah again makes night a garment, then pairs it with sleep and the day's rising, giving the section's worn night-cover its daily function.
The exact source-section gesture appears: people يَسْتَغْشُونَ ثِيَابَهُمْ while trying to conceal themselves, yet Allah knows their secret and public speech.
Noah's hearers block their ears and wrap themselves in their clothes, so the garment concretely becomes refusal of the warner.
The ayah first gives clothing for nakedness and adornment, then declares لِبَاسُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ better, explicitly joining the section's outer robe and inward protective layer.
The shirts تَقِيكُمُ heat and armor protects in battle; this is the section's literal Quranic meeting of a garment with the protecting sense of و ق ي.
Night is sworn by إِذَا يَغْشَىٰهَا, repeating the source ayah's covering action while giving that action an object.
Allah يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ, presenting night as a cover drawn over day rather than merely a time after it.
The repeated formula يُغْشِى ٱلَّيْلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ supplies another direct cosmic staging of the section's night-cover.
When night جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ, Abraham is enclosed by it before seeing the star; the ayah makes the human viewpoint inside the night-cover perceptible.
Allah makes drowsiness يَغْشِّيكُم as security and follows it with purification and strengthened hearts, a benevolent covering that genuinely protects inwardly.
In the setting of the fasting night, spouses are called reciprocal clothing, هُنَّ لِبَاسٌ لَّكُمْ وَأَنتُمْ لِبَاسٌ لَّهُنَّ, combining night, bodily enclosure, intimacy, and concealment.
Allah teaches David the making of لَبُوسٍ that protects people from violence, an unambiguous garment whose value lies in protection rather than display.
The condemned speaker says مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ, almost exactly restaging the section's claim that wealth avails nothing at the fall.
مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ directly repeats the failure of a hostile rich man's wealth to protect him.
What misers withheld will be طَوَّقُوا۟, collared around their necks on Resurrection; hoarded wealth becomes the fatal thing worn on the body.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend receive a warning of punishment, directly opposing the giver whose inward garment is taqwa.
The hoarded metal from 9:34 is heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, turning carried wealth into a fiery covering on the body.
Wealth and children are زِينَةُ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا while lasting deeds are better, precisely distinguishing the decorative robe from what remains.
Worldly life is described as adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth before becoming dry debris, exposing the short life of the robe made from possessions.
Qarun comes before his people فِى زِينَتِهِۦ, making wealth's public display into the visible ornamental robe imagined by the section.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no company can protect him; the adornment of 28:79 fails at the precise moment of downfall.
After listing lavish fittings, the ayah calls them mere worldly زُخْرُفًا and reserves the Hereafter for the muttaqin, directly opposing ornament to taqwa.
Wealth and children will not avail against Allah, and their owners become fuel for the Fire, joining failed possessions to the threatened flame in one ayah.
The same no-avail formula for wealth and children ends with abiding in the Fire, a direct parallel to the section's useless robe at destruction.
Neither wealth nor children avail against Allah, and the people concerned are companions of the Fire; possession supplies no protective layer.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth embodies the self-sufficient wearer of the section's ornamental robe.
He supposes his wealth has made him immortal, explicitly mistaking possessions for protection before the rejection in 104:4.
The blaze identified in 70:15 calls the one who gathered wealth and withheld it, reproducing the miser-to-fire movement behind the section's two garments.
قُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا commands active protection from fire with the same و ق ي root that the section hears as a protective cloth.
فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ makes the taqwa verb itself the commanded protection from fire, the exact relation the section draws between 92:5 and the flame.
وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ again directly names taqwa as protection against a prepared fire.
Allah saves those who practiced taqwa and leaves the wrongdoers kneeling in Hell, matching the inward garment's actual rescue from the flame.
Allah delivers those who had taqwa so that evil does not touch them, stating the protective efficacy that the source section renders as an unseen cloth.
The people of the Garden are وَوَقَىٰهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, explicitly protected by Allah from Hell with the section's protection root.
Amid their enjoyment, their Lord وَوَقَىٰهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, making rescue from flame the ground beneath the visible reward.
The saved say Allah favored them and وَوَقَىٰنَا عَذَابَ ٱلسَّمُومِ, a first-person statement of the protective layer against scorching punishment.
The angels ask Allah to وَقِهِمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ, using the source root for direct protection from Hell.
The prayer وَقِهِمُ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ then defines such protection on that Day as mercy, bringing out the inward moral work of the section's vikāya.
The prayer وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ asks for precisely the protection from fire that the section's taqwa-garment supplies.
Believers ask وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, keeping the protection root and fire in the same short plea.
Those who remember and reflect conclude فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ, showing the inward stance that seeks the true covering.
The ayah joins taqwa, listening, obedience, spending, and being يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ; protection here is specifically protection from the avarice of the section's miser.
Those who prefer others despite need are يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ, so generosity itself discloses an inward protection from possessiveness.
Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and publicly, bring the section's night-cover, hidden inner act, and giving into one formulation.
Concealed alms to the poor are better and erase evils, directly favoring a hidden protective good over visible display.
Giving food despite love for it to the needy, orphan, and captive concretely enacts the generous wearer of the section's inward garment.
The givers seek only Allah's Face and no repayment or thanks, identifying the unseen motive beneath the act in 76:8.
Their fear of a grim Day supplies the taqwa-like inward stance that links the giving of 76:8-9 to protection.
Allah وَقَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمِ, making protection the direct consequence of the preceding gift, intention, and fear.
The protected givers are rewarded with Garden and silk, so a true outward garment follows the inward protection of 76:11.
The surah of the enwrapped night-worshipper ends by joining alms with a good loan to Allah, uniting night, garment, gift, and the section's debt-sense of the robe.
Moses is warned not to be turned from the Hour فَتَرْدَىٰ, using the source root in its ruin/perishing sense and tying that ruin to heedless desire.
A person in Paradise tells his former companion إِن كِدتَّ لَتُرْدِينِ, using the same root for nearly bringing someone to ruin through denial.
The false assumption people held about their Lord أَرْدَىٰكُمْ, ruined them, showing an inward cause of the downfall named by the source root.
After the fall, Adam and his spouse fasten garden leaves over their exposed bodies; this is the loss-of-covering scene that immediately precedes 7:26's two garments.
Allah يُكَوِّرُ night over day and day over night, using the action of wrapping one layer around another to stage the cosmic garment nonlexically.
Their shirts are pitch and fire covers their faces, the source section's explicit inverse garment: what is worn and what covers both intensify the burning.
ثِيَابٌ مِّن نَّارٍ are cut out for the disputants, turning the protective function of clothing into its exact opposite.
Allah makes a secure, well-provided town taste لِبَاسَ ٱلْجُوعِ وَٱلْخَوْفِ, showing that a garment can also be an enveloping punishment after ingratitude.
Satan strips the first parents of their clothing to expose them, setting the loss of an outer cover against the better taqwa-garment named in 7:26.
Faces appear covered with pieces of dark night; the benign cosmic garment becomes an image of disgrace from which there is no protector.
Hell is a bed with غَوَاشٍ above its people, converting an enclosing cover into punishment rather than shelter.
A غَاشِيَةٌ of Allah's punishment may come suddenly, using the covering root for an overwhelming threat rather than protective clothing.
Punishment يَغْشَىٰهُم from above and beneath their feet, an all-enclosing anti-garment.
Layers of fire stand above and below Hell's people, a complete fiery enclosure opposed to the unseen cloth that guards from flame.
The condemned person can only يَتَّقِى بِوَجْهِهِۦ the terrible punishment, a bitter reversal in which the exposed face must serve as an inadequate shield.
Those who consume orphans' wealth eat fire into their bellies, turning acquired property into an inward burning rather than an inward protection.
The wealth-counter of 104:2-3 is cast into the Crusher, decisively breaking his belief that wealth preserves him.
The Crusher of 104:4 is identified as Allah's kindled fire, completing the rich man's movement from counted wealth to flame.
The man whose wealth fails in 111:2 enters a flaming fire, completing the same no-protection sequence as the source section.
Those who wanted worldly life and its adornment in 11:15 have only the Fire in the Hereafter, exposing ornamental success as a garment that cannot endure.
A building founded on a crumbling edge collapses with its builder into Hellfire, a nonlexical staging of support and self-made security becoming a fall.
The sea فَغَشِيَهُم with what covered them, using the covering root for a fatal engulfing instead of shelter.
Allah فَأَغْشَيْنَـٰهُمْ so they cannot see; the self-chosen garment of refusal becomes a divinely imposed covering of perception.
The enwrapped person of 73:1 is commanded to rise in the night, so entering the night-cover becomes wakeful obedience rather than concealment from a warning.
The cloaked person of 74:1 is told قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ, reversing the people who wrap their garments to evade the warner.
Charity displayed for people is like dust stripped from a rock and yields nothing, a precise image of an impressive outer layer with no protective inner substance.
Spending to be seen by people supplies the outward act without faith, the opposite of the section's quiet inner layer of giving and taqwa.
Those who merely show their worship embody visible display without the inward protective quality the section assigns to taqwa.
The show-offs of 107:6 also withhold small aid, joining outward appearance to the miser's refusal to give.
The address يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُزَّمِّلُ presents a person physically enwrapped, the human-scale counterpart to the section's night worn as a garment.
The address يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلْمُدَّثِّرُ likewise begins with a cloaked person and makes the posture of being wrapped morally open to what follows.

وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ places the cleansing of garments beside the cloaked warner's commission, inviting the section's relation between outer dress and inward readiness without deciding the phrase's full scope.
Women are told to draw their outer cloaks close so they may be recognized and not harmed, giving the jilbab a concrete protective role akin to the source dictionary's vikāya layer.
Drawing head-coverings over the bosom and not displaying adornment joins a worn cover to the concealment of ornament, clarifying the section's quiet layer beneath show.
Older women may set aside outer garments without displaying adornment, yet restraint is better; the ayah marks a boundary between the garment itself and the inward quality.
David is told to make full coats of mail and measure their links, supplying the crafted layers of the protective clothing whose purpose 21:80 states.
Paradise is promised as a place where Adam will not be naked, preparing the covering-loss scene in 20:121.
Adam will not suffer the sun's heat in Paradise, identifying the exposure from which clothing protects before the fall.
After disobedience, the pair's nakedness appears and they patch on garden leaves, repeating the fall-and-cover scene behind 7:22-26.
Day is stripped نَسْلَخُ from night and people are left in darkness, a garment-like removal that complements night being laid over the world.
A غِشَـٰوَةٌ lies over sight after hearts and hearing are sealed, internalizing the covering used in the section to avoid seeing and hearing truth.
Allah places غِشَـٰوَةً over the sight of one who takes desire as a god, presenting perceptual covering as the result of inward self-sufficiency.
Rejecters answer the messenger that their hearts are in coverings, their ears heavy, and a barrier stands between them, verbalizing the refusal enacted by wrapping in clothes.
One reminded of the signs turns away, while coverings lie over hearts and heaviness in ears; it is a nonliteral counterpart to the source's clothed evasion of warning.
Coverings on hearts and heaviness in ears culminate in people turning their backs when the one Lord is mentioned, closely matching concealment joined to turning away.
Some listen while coverings on their hearts and heaviness in their ears prevent understanding, restaging the blocked hearing of Noah's clothed hearers inwardly.
People put fingers in their ears against thunderclaps from fear of death, repeating Noah's hearers' exact bodily gesture in a storm rather than in response to preaching.
A wave يَغْشَىٰهُ another wave with cloud above produces darkness upon darkness, a layered natural covering that helps picture the section's hidden intermediate layer.
The speaker's authority has perished immediately after his wealth avails nothing in 69:28, extending the failure from possession to status.
The Day when neither wealth nor children benefit states the same boundary on material protection without staging the fall itself.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, giving voice to the self-sufficient stance beneath the decorative robe.
His produce is destroyed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while the trellises lie collapsed, making prosperous display end in visible downfall.
No company can help the ruined owner besides Allah and he cannot defend himself, stating why the collapsed wealth of 18:42 was no covering.
The affluent claim that greater wealth and children mean they will not be punished, explicitly treating possessions as a shield.
Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to Allah; faith and good action do, separating outward possession from the inward basis of safety.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment can receive their works there, identifying the decorative object whose final failure 11:16 reveals.
The earth takes on its adornment and its people think they control it just before Allah's command leaves it mown down, a large-scale version of ornament mistaken for security.
Worldly gifts are enjoyment and adornment, while what is with Allah is better and more lasting, setting the robe's passing glitter against what endures.
The Prophet is told not to let his eyes pass beyond sincere worshippers seeking the adornment of worldly life, preferring the hidden orientation over visible finery.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the flower of worldly life; his Lord's provision is better and more lasting, another boundary around decorative possession.
What people possess runs out while what is with Allah remains, stating the temporal difference between the failing worn ornament and genuine security.
Those who spend secretly and publicly hope for a commerce that never perishes, converting relinquished wealth into the lasting asset the decorative robe cannot be.
Following the command to spend and the protection from avarice in 64:16, a good loan to Allah is multiplied and forgiven; giving reverses the source dictionary's robe-as-debt.
Charitable men and women are described as lending Allah a good loan that is multiplied, turning parted wealth into credit rather than carrying it as liability.
Some Bedouins regard expenditure as a financial burden and await misfortune, exposing the miser's construal of giving as debt.
Others regard expenditure as nearness to Allah and the Messenger's prayers, reversing 9:98's burden and clarifying what giving can become inwardly.
The question whether the hearers are مُّثْقَلُونَ مِن مَّغْرَمٍ pictures an imposed payment as weight, giving concrete force to the source dictionary's debt worn like a robe.
The repeated phrase مُّثْقَلُونَ مِن مَّغْرَمٍ again makes liability something that weighs a person down, close to the section's shoulder-borne debt image.
A debtor in hardship is to receive respite, and remission is better charity; this treats debt as a burden relieved by giving rather than an adornment retained.

Because dayn is only the source dictionary's secondary sense of ridā, the command to record a fixed-term debt supplies a semantic boundary: the obligation remains real even when not outwardly visible.
True righteousness includes giving loved wealth to vulnerable people and ends by naming such people the muttaqin, directly coupling gift with taqwa.
People will not attain righteousness until they spend from what they love, placing inner moral gain in surrendering the would-be ornament.
The Garden is prepared for the muttaqin, and the next ayah identifies them through spending, making taqwa the protection beneath generosity.
Those who spend in ease and hardship are the muttaqin introduced in 3:133, a direct parallel to the section's giver who practices taqwa.
Neither sacrificial flesh nor blood reaches Allah, but taqwa from people does, sharply distinguishing the unseen inward reality from a visible material form.
Spending for Allah's pleasure and from inner certainty is likened to a fruitful garden, supplying the inward counterpart to the showy spending stripped bare in 2:264.
Allah protects the believer from the evils of Pharaoh's plot, while the punishment surrounds Pharaoh's people, showing effective protection immediately before their fire scene.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, specifying the danger from which the believer of 40:45 was protected.
Those for whom good has preceded are kept far from Hell, a nonlexical equivalent of the section's most protected person being spared the flame.
The saved are clothed in green silk and adorned with silver bracelets; following 76:8-12, visible dress arrives as gift after inward giving, fear, and protection.
Whoever defrauds will carry what was taken on Resurrection, turning secretly acquired wealth into a bodily borne liability rather than protective adornment.
One who associates partners is likened to a person falling from the sky and being snatched or swept away, a nonlexical picture of the source root's fatal descent.
The righteous are adorned and wear green silk in the lasting Garden, a bestowed robe that contrasts with wealth worn as self-made worldly security.
Believers are adorned with gold and pearls and their clothing is silk, locating true outward adornment after divine entry into the Garden.
The people entering the everlasting Garden receive bracelets, pearls, and silk garments, another robe bestowed after salvation rather than relied on before it.
Allah appoints night for repose while breaking open the dawn, giving the section's night-garment a concrete function as an enclosing interval of rest.
Night is made so people may rest in it and day so they may see, clarifying what the benign night-cover enables.
The repeated sign of night for rest and day for visibility places covering darkness and exposure to sight in a purposeful pair.
The question who could bring night in which people rest if day were perpetual marks the life-giving boundary supplied by the night-cover.
Allah again makes night for rest and day for sight, presenting darkness as a provided shelter rather than mere absence of light.
People extract ornaments from the sea that they wear, supplying a literal Quranic instance of material provision becoming bodily adornment like the source dictionary's robe.
The repeated sea scene yields ornaments that people wear, concretizing the section's secondary definition of whatever adorns a person as their robe.
Moses says Pharaoh and his chiefs were given adornment and wealth in worldly life and used it to lead astray, joining visible finery, possession, and moral ruin.
Qarun's treasure keys burden a strong company, making his wealth physically weighty before it appears publicly as adornment.
Qarun claims his wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, voicing the self-sufficiency behind the ornament displayed in 28:79.
Those given knowledge answer the spectators of Qarun's adornment that Allah's reward is better for believers who act rightly.
After Qarun's fall, yesterday's admirers recognize that wealth's expansion is Allah's test and that unbelievers do not prosper, stating the scene's correction.
The rich garden owner enters his estate while wronging himself and asserts that it will never perish, explicitly treating displayed wealth as lasting protection.
He doubts the Hour and expects an even better return if brought back, extending the false security of his ornament beyond death.
His companion tells him to acknowledge Allah's will and that there is no power except through Allah, naming the stance absent from the self-worn robe.
Pharaoh demands to know why Moses has not been given gold bracelets or an angelic retinue, treating worn ornament as proof of authority.
After Pharaoh's display-based challenge, Allah drowns him and his people, showing the impotence of the status ornament invoked in 43:53.
The garden owners resolve that no poor person will enter upon them, giving a concrete form to the withholding stance of the section's miser.
On finding their garden ruined, the owners recognize that they themselves have been deprived, reversing the security they sought by excluding the poor.
A fiber rope is around the neck of the household that trusted wealth, an exact bodily counter-image in which what is worn signifies liability and punishment.
The speaker whose wealth and authority failed is seized and shackled, so his former possessions end in an imposed bodily binding.
He is then burned in Hell, completing the movement from failed wealth in 69:28 to the fire against which it supplied no cover.
The passage identifies failure to urge feeding the poor among the condemned man's offenses, linking his useless wealth to withheld generosity.
The kindled fire following the wealth-counter rises over the hearts, replacing the inward protective layer with inward-reaching flame.
The fire is closed over its people, forming an imprisoning cover around the one who mistook accumulated wealth for security.
Hell already encompasses the unbelievers before 29:55 depicts punishment covering them from above and below, completing the anti-garment enclosure.
What covered the overturned towns covered them utterly; although the wording leaves the agent undescribed, the source root again denotes a fatal covering.
The Hereafter's punishment is harder and there is no وَاقٍ from Allah, marking the limit beyond which no self-chosen covering can protect.
Earlier peoples had greater strength and monuments, yet Allah seized them and they had no protector, joining failed outward power to the absence of true vikāya.
On the Day people turn their backs fleeing, no one can protect them from Allah, setting a boundary on every merely external defense.
Allah saves those who believed and practiced taqwa from the destroyed settlement, showing taqwa's protective result in an earthly judgment.
Those who believed and practiced taqwa are rescued from the punishing blast, another concrete deliverance attributed to the inward stance.
The command to spend is immediately joined to the warning not to cast oneself into destruction, directly coupling giving with avoidance of the fatal fall.
Good expenditure benefits the giver and is made only in seeking Allah's Face, identifying the hidden intention beneath the source section's generous act.
Charity taken from wealth purifies and causes growth, explaining how giving possessions supplies an inward cleansing rather than an outward ornament.
Those who seek their Lord's Face spend secretly and publicly and repel evil with good, joining concealed generosity to moral protection.
Believers are commanded to spend secretly and publicly before a Day when trade cannot help, distinguishing present giving from wealth that later fails.
A gift intended to increase through people brings no increase with Allah, while alms seeking His Face multiplies, separating outward financial return from inwardly directed giving.
In the same passage where fire calls the collector who withheld, the prayerful have a recognized share within their wealth, presenting the opposite relation to possession.
That fixed share belongs to the petitioner and deprived, specifying the giving that answers the hoarder's failure in 70:18.
The people of Saqar admit they did not feed the poor, tying the fire announced in the cloaked warner's surah to withheld provision.
The rebuked people do not urge one another to feed the poor, giving a social form to the miser's refusal.
They love wealth with consuming love, stating the inward attachment that turns possessions into the section's deceptive robe.
Hell is brought into view after the rebuke over the poor and love of wealth, completing the same possession-to-fire sequence.
The best provision is taqwa, another Quranic image of inward protection as something carried for a journey rather than worn for display.
The most honored person before Allah is the most possessed of taqwa, relocating distinction from visible status and adornment to the inward quality.
A good loan to Allah is multiplied many times, reversing the dictionary's robe-as-debt by making relinquished wealth a lasting credit.
The question who will lend Allah a good loan promises multiplication and a noble reward, again transforming wealth from carried liability into gift.
Within the covenant, establishing prayer and alms is joined to lending Allah a good loan, placing the debt image on the side of generous fidelity.
People are told to take their adornment at worship but not be excessive, providing a boundary in which outward dress is legitimate without becoming self-sufficient display.
Allah's adornment and good provisions are not forbidden, but are purely for believers in the Hereafter, distinguishing gifted beauty from the false protective use of ornament.
The cloaked warner is told not to give in pursuit of greater return, supplying an inward rule for giving beside the command to purify his garments.
